item.mechanism: Ultrafine-grain microstructure enhances oxidation resistance by increasing the density of grain boundaries (GBs), which act as short-circuit diffusion paths for Cr ions to reach the surface rapidly, forming a continuous, protective Cr2O3 layer that limits further oxidation.
item.system: AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy processed by stationary friction processing (SFP) at 1800 rpm (SFP_1800) resulting in an average grain size of 0.43 μm with a bimodal distribution and ~54% nanograins.
item.operating_conditions: Oxidation in laboratory air at 850–1050 °C for 100 h; processing involved SFP at 1800 rpm for 5 min with peak temperatures up to ~780 °C and strain rates up to 1130.90 s–1.
item.supporting_observation: The SFP_1800 sample showed a 38–48% reduction in oxidation kinetics compared to the as-cast sample, with a dense, adherent Cr2O3 scale and high activation energy for oxidation.
item.scope_limits: The mechanism relies on the presence of high-angle grain boundaries and specific elemental composition (Al, Cr) to form chromia; it does not hold for the as-cast coarse-grained sample where slow diffusion leads to non-protective spinel formation.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors considered that low diffusion in coarse grains leads to the formation of brittle, non-protective spinel oxides (CoCr2O4, FeCr2O4) which cause cracking and poor protection.
quotes: High density GBs facilitate rapid oxidation of chromium cations and form continuous chromia protective scales, which limit the oxidation kinetics over a period of time.
The poor oxidation behavior of the as-cast samples is due to the formation of a nonadherent mixed oxide layer (spinel) above the alumina scale owing to the low diffusion of elements through GBs.

item.mechanism: High surface free energy (SFE) in ultrafine-grain microstructures suppresses the formation of non-protective spinel oxides and promotes the selective formation of protective chromia and alumina scales.
item.system: AlCoCrFeNi HEA processed by SFP at 1800 rpm (SFP_1800) and 400 rpm (SFP_400), exhibiting SFE increases of 35.2% and 29.8% respectively compared to the as-cast state.
item.operating_conditions: Oxidation in laboratory air at 850–1050 °C for 100 h; SFE measured via contact angle with water and ethanol on polished surfaces.
item.supporting_observation: Processed samples showed primarily Al2O3 and Cr2O3 with only minor spinel peaks, whereas as-cast samples formed significant amounts of CoCr2O4 and FeCr2O4 spinels.
item.scope_limits: The suppression of spinels is attributed to high SFE; the text does not quantify the exact SFE threshold required for this suppression in other alloy systems.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors note that typically ultrafine-grained samples with high SFE are prone to oxygen attack due to defects, but in this specific alloy, the SFE favors protective scale formation over spinel formation.
quotes: The likely reason for the lack of spinel species in the processed samples is the high surface free energy, which suppresses the formation of spinel oxides.
Total SFE of a sample reflects the combined effects of the dispersive and polar components, but the effect of the polar component is dominant over that of the dispersive component.

item.mechanism: Ultrafine-grain microstructure promotes internal oxidation by providing short-circuit diffusion channels (high GB density) that allow inward flux of oxygen ions to react with metallic ions deep within the alloy, forming an Al-rich internal oxide zone (IOZ).
item.system: AlCoCrFeNi HEA processed by SFP at 1800 rpm (SFP_1800) and 400 rpm (SFP_400), characterized by average grain sizes of 0.43 μm and 1 μm respectively.
item.operating_conditions: Oxidation in laboratory air at 950–1050 °C for 100 h; observed in cross-sectional BSE images and EDS maps.
item.supporting_observation: Ultrafine-grained samples oxidized at 950 and 1050 °C showed a considerable internal oxidation zone (IOZ) with Al-rich oxides, unlike the as-cast sample.
item.scope_limits: This mechanism is specific to samples with high strain rates and high GB density; the as-cast sample with coarse grains did not exhibit this significant internal oxidation zone.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors contrast this with the as-cast sample where low GB density restricts inward oxygen diffusion, preventing the formation of a deep internal oxidation zone.
quotes: Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides.

Inner oxides are more likely to form in samples processed at high strain rate, since short circuit diffusion channels and high SFE sites are provided by the high intensity GBs present in the ultrafine-grained samples.
These channels aid the inward flux of O ions to react with the metallic ions and form the internal oxides.

item.mechanism: Dynamic recrystallization driven by high strain rate and peak temperature during stationary friction processing (SFP) refines the grain structure and induces a phase transformation from BCC/B2 to FCC, which contributes to the enhanced oxidation resistance.
item.system: AlCoCrFeNi HEA processed by SFP at 400 rpm (SFP_400) and 1800 rpm (SFP_1800).
item.operating_conditions: SFP processing for 5 min at rotational speeds of 400 rpm (peak temp ~320 °C) and 1800 rpm (peak temp ~780 °C); oxidation tested at 850–1050 °C.
item.supporting_observation: The SFP_1800 sample showed a 55% FCC phase fraction compared to 38% in SFP_400, and the grain size decreased from 98 μm (as-cast) to 0.43 μm.
item.scope_limits: The phase transformation is attributed to the specific combination of high strain rate and temperature during SFP; the text does not claim this transformation occurs without severe deformation.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors note that the evolution of the FCC phase is likely due to the significant increase in defect density (dislocations, point defects, GB fraction) increasing system energy.
quotes: The evolution of refined microstructure during processing is attributed to dynamic recrystallization, which is a function of strain-rate and peak temperature.
The evolution of the FCC phase is likely due to BCC/B2 phase transformation into FCC during high strain-rate processing.
The highly refined grain structure of SFP_1800 sample is attributed to high strain-rate deformation resulting in dynamic recrystallization.

item.mechanism: The effective diffusion coefficient increases as grain size decreases, accelerating the formation of a continuous protective oxide layer by enhancing intergranular diffusion of mobile atoms.
item.system: AlCoCrFeNi HEA with varying grain sizes: as-cast (98 μm), SFP_400 (1 μm), and SFP_1800 (0.43 μm).
item.operating_conditions: Oxidation in laboratory air at 850–1050 °C for 100 h; diffusion analysis based on grain size dependence.
item.supporting_observation: The calculated effective diffusion coefficient ratio (D/D*) increased significantly as grain size decreased, correlating with the observed reduction in oxidation kinetics.
item.scope_limits: This relationship is derived from a model summing GB and lattice diffusion; it assumes the grain size is the primary variable affecting the diffusion coefficient.
item.alternatives_considered: The text implies that without the high density of GBs (as in coarse grains), the diffusion is too slow to form a continuous protective layer quickly, leading to mixed oxides.
quotes: The decrease in grain size is attributed to the enhanced intergranular diffusion of mobile atoms owing to high number of GBs, which would accelerate the formation of a continuous layer due to the high diffusivity of ionic species.
An effective diffusion coefficient ( D ), which is a sum of GB diffusion and lattice diffusion coefficient, was analyzed to explain this.
Grain size dependence of the effective diffusion coefficient is plotted as shown in Figure 11 using eq 4 and shows the increase in effective diffusion coefficient with the decrease in the grain size.

item.mechanism: The formation of a dense, layered oxide scale consisting of top chromia and inner alumina acts as a barrier to the oxidation process, providing high oxidation resistance.
item.system: AlCoCrFeNi HEA processed by SFP at 1800 rpm (SFP_1800) and 400 rpm (SFP_400).
item.operating_conditions: Oxidation in laboratory air at 850–1050 °C for 100 h; scale structure analyzed via cross-sectional BSE and EDS.
item.supporting_observation: Processed samples showed a densely packed and well-adherent oxide scale with a layered structure, whereas as-cast samples had cracked, non-adherent mixed oxide layers.
item.scope_limits: The mechanism depends on the specific thermodynamic stability of Al2O3 and Cr2O3 in this alloy system; the text notes that spinels are detrimental and reduce protectiveness.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors argue that the as-cast sample's failure is due to the formation of non-adherent mixed oxide layers (spinel) which fail to restrict cation/anion accumulation.
quotes: Formation of this dense layered structure act as a barrier for the oxidation process to proceed further, which provide high oxidation resistance to the processed samples.
The oxide scale of both the samples is composed of a layered structure with top chromia and aluminum-rich inner oxides.
These brittle spinels are detrimental as they reduce the protectiveness of the oxide scale and undermine interfacial adhesion.

item.mechanism: Higher rotational speeds during stationary friction processing lead to deeper depth of refinement (DOR) and higher strain rates, which result in more significant grain refinement and phase transformation, thereby enhancing oxidation resistance.
item.system: AlCoCrFeNi HEA processed by SFP at 400 rpm (DOR 300–650 μm, grain size 1 μm) vs. 1800 rpm (DOR 300–650 μm, grain size 0.43 μm).
item.operating_conditions: SFP for 5 min at 400 rpm (avg temp ~280 °C) and 1800 rpm (avg temp ~760 °C); oxidation at 850–1050 °C.
item.supporting_observation: SFP_1800 showed a 38–48% reduction in oxidation kinetics compared to 12–20% for SFP_400, correlating with the higher strain rate and finer grain size.
item.scope_limits: The benefit is dependent on the rotational speed; the text does not discuss the effects of speeds outside the 400–1800 rpm range.
item.alternatives_considered: The text suggests that the increment in DOR with rotational speed is due to the thick column of plastically deformed zone during processing at higher rotation speed.
quotes: The increment in DOR with rotational speed is likely due to the thick column of plastically deformed zone during processing at higher rotation speed.
High temperature at higher rotational speed favors the material flow through thermal softening and leads to deeper DOR.
The SFP_400 sample showed a 12–20% reduction in the oxidation kinetics, whereas the SFP_1800 sample showed a 38–48% reduction in the oxidation kinetics compared to the as-cast alloy.

item.mechanism: The thermodynamic stability of oxides dictates the layering order, with Al2O3 forming at the bottom due to its highest Gibbs free energy of formation and Cr2O3 forming at the top due to its lower free energy, creating a protective barrier.
item.system: AlCoCrFeNi HEA processed by SFP (SFP_400 and SFP_1800) and as-cast.
item.operating_conditions: Oxidation in laboratory air at 850–1050 °C for 100 h; thermodynamic properties calculated using FactsageEdu73 software.
item.supporting_observation: The order of formation was determined by Gibbs free energy: Al2O3 (−903.88 kJ/mol) forms the bottom layer, while Cr2O3 (−574.26 kJ/mol) forms the top layer in processed samples.
item.scope_limits: This mechanism relies on the specific thermodynamic data for Al and Cr in this alloy; the text notes that spinels form in as-cast samples due to kinetic limitations rather than thermodynamic preference.
item.alternatives_considered: The authors state that the poor oxidation behavior of as-cast samples is due to the formation of non-adherent mixed oxide layers (spinel) above the alumina scale, which is a kinetic outcome of low diffusion.
quotes: The order of formation of various metal oxides is governed by their thermodynamic properties, given by Gibbs free energy at a specific temperature.
